# Preface {.unnumbered}

Version: {{< meta version >}}

Welcome to *Data Science in Engineering*, a master's course at Trier University of Applied Sciences for students of mechanical engineering, electrical engineering and industrial engineering.

## What this course is about

Every method in this script is introduced together with a real, publicly available engineering dataset – from power plants and gas turbines to rolling bearings, semiconductor production and jet engines. Theory and practice go hand in hand: each chapter starts with a (fictional) engineering scenario that calls for a decision, explains the methods needed to make it, applies them in Python – and returns to the scenario at the end to make the decision with the results.

The course has four parts:

| Part | Topics | Chapters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A – Understanding Data | workflow, exploratory analysis, data quality | 1–2 |
| B – Statistical Inference | probability and uncertainty, hypothesis tests, regression, design of experiments | 3–5 |
| C – Prediction and Monitoring | model selection and validation, classification, ensembles, unsupervised learning | 6–9 |
| D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning | from diagnosis to prognosis: signal features, forecasting, remaining useful life with neural networks; review | 10–13 |

Before Part A, the short lesson [Getting Started with pandas](notebooks/00-pandas.ipynb) introduces the Python library pandas for everyone who has not used it before.

## What you will be able to do

By the end of the course, you will be able to tackle an engineering question you have not seen before with data – on your own and from start to finish: prepare real measurement data, choose and validate suitable methods from statistics or machine learning, and derive a recommendation for a decision. A good analysis quantifies the uncertainty of its results and explains the recommendation – including the limits of data and model – so that others can follow and check it.

Engineers increasingly face exactly such questions: Is a test result strong enough to confirm a claimed improvement? Can a cheaper concrete mix be approved before any specimens exist? Is a failure alarm worth its false alarms? Which safety margin does a lifetime prediction need? The scenarios of the chapters are modelled on situations like these.

The course builds up this ability along the steps of such an analysis:

1. **Translate the question** into a data science task: target, influencing variables, type of task, and the information available at the time of the decision.
2. **Check and prepare the data:** judge whether a dataset is fit for the question, and clean it (Part A).
3. **Quantify effects and uncertainty** with statistical models: how precisely is a value known, and is an effect statistically established and practically relevant? (Part B)
4. **Build and validate prediction and monitoring models:** does a model meet the requirements of a specific use on new data? (Part C)
5. **Respect the order in time** of signals, time series and sensor sequences (Part D).
6. **Justify a recommendation** – with its uncertainty, its assumptions and the limits of data and model. Every chapter practises this in the section *Back to the decision*.

The first step runs through the whole course: choosing an approach requires the methods of Parts B to D, and Chapter 13 brings them together. The learning goals at the start of each chapter name the smaller steps.

## Prerequisites

Basic Python programming and mathematics at bachelor level (linear algebra, calculus, introductory statistics). If you have not worked with the Python library pandas before, start with the short introduction [Getting Started with pandas](notebooks/00-pandas.ipynb) before Chapter 1.

## How to work with this script

The script is meant to be read in the browser or as a PDF. Every result in it was computed with Python, and the code is part of the script: in the HTML version, click *Code* above a result to show it. You can copy it into your own notebook to reproduce or vary an analysis.

During the semester, the demo code from the lectures is provided as Jupyter notebooks.

### Software

You can work with any development environment you like (e.g. JupyterLab, VS Code or PyCharm), as long as it can open, run and edit Jupyter notebooks. We recommend Google Colab; a local installation is an alternative:

- **Google Colab (recommended):** [Colab](https://colab.research.google.com) runs notebooks in the browser – no installation required, on a laptop or a tablet (an external keyboard helps a lot). Sign in with a Google account and open a notebook via *File → Upload notebook*. Most packages used in this course are pre-installed. Files you download or upload in Colab live only as long as the session; save results you want to keep to Google Drive or download them.
- **Alternative – local installation:** The [Anaconda Distribution](https://www.anaconda.com/download) installs Python, Jupyter and the most important data science packages in one go – a good choice if you prefer to work offline and with files on your own computer.

Packages that are missing can be installed directly from a notebook cell with `%pip install`, e.g. `%pip install ucimlrepo`.

**Optional: keep the data in Colab.** The notebooks download each dataset once into a folder `data` in the current working directory. In Colab, this folder disappears with the session, so the data are downloaded again the next time. If you want to avoid this, run the following cell at the start of a notebook: the folder `data` is then created in your Google Drive and kept. The cell works only in Colab.

```python
from google.colab import drive
drive.mount("/content/drive")                        # asks once for permission to access Drive
%mkdir -p "/content/drive/MyDrive/Data Science"      # course folder in Drive (created if missing)
%cd "/content/drive/MyDrive/Data Science"            # work there: ./data is now in Drive
```

### Reading guide

Each chapter opens with a scenario (purple box) and closes it in a section *Back to the decision*. The people and situations are invented; the data are real (or, where stated, simulated).

Coloured boxes highlight what matters most:

::: {.callout-note}
## Definitions
Blue boxes define the central concepts.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key results
Red boxes contain theorems, key results and the takeaways at the end of each chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfalls
Yellow boxes warn of typical mistakes – in data science, many of them lead to results that look convincing but are wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Engineering practice
Green boxes give practical advice for engineering projects.
:::

Each chapter ends with exercises (highlighted boxes) followed by **solutions**, which are collapsed in the HTML version – try the exercise first, then open the solution. The lab assignments of the course build on the exercises.

Sections and exercises marked **Extension** go beyond the core of the course. They are optional and not required for the exam – use them to dig deeper into topics that matter for your own work.

### Notation

The script uses the following conventions throughout:

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| $x_1, \dots, x_n$ | observations (sample of size $n$); $x_i$ is the $i$-th observation |
| $\bar x$, $s$ | sample mean and sample standard deviation |
| $\tilde x$ | sample median |
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ | mean and standard deviation of the population or distribution |
| $\hat\theta$ | estimate of a parameter $\theta$ (the hat marks anything computed from data) |
| $y$, $\hat y$ | response (target) and its prediction |
| $X$ | matrix of inputs: one row per observation, one column per input |
| $P(A)$, $P(A \mid B)$ | probability, conditional probability |
| $E[X]$, $\text{Var}(X)$ | expected value and variance of a random variable $X$ |
| $\ln$ | natural logarithm |

The Greek alphabet is small, and the standard symbols of different fields overlap. Where a symbol has different meanings in different chapters, the meaning is stated where it is used. The most important cases: $\beta$ is the Weibull shape parameter (Chapter 3), the probability of a type II error (Chapter 4) and a regression coefficient (Chapters 5–7); $\eta$ is the Weibull scale parameter (Chapter 3) and the learning rate (Chapter 12); $\sigma$ denotes a standard deviation and, in Chapters 7 and 12, an activation function.

## Assessment

- **Lab assignments** (coursework, pass/fail): four assignments during the semester.
- **Written exam** (90 minutes, without computer): method choice, interpretation of results, justified decisions, short calculations and code reading.

Passing the lab assignments is the prerequisite for admission to the written exam.

In the exam, you may use the [Python Quick Reference](python-reference.qmd) and the [Formula Collection](formulas.qmd) from the appendix. Both are handed out with the exam; your own copies or notes are not allowed.
